title: When Values Become Identity
summary: We do not always defend a position only because we think it is true. Sometimes we also like what believing it says about us. A value can slowly become an identity — “I am humanist,” “I am feminist,” “I am rational” — until contradicting the position begins to feel like contradicting the person. The French radical left offers a revealing case of what can happen when a political movement comes to see itself as the natural bearer of humanism, emancipation and universal rights.
body:
I. The position in which we admire ourselves

There are opinions we hold, and there are opinions in which we begin to recognize ourselves.

The distinction seems small. Compare “I value humanism” with “I am a humanist.” In the first sentence, humanism remains a principle outside myself, something I use to judge my actions. In the second, it has become something I believe about myself. I am humane. I care about dignity. I belong to the side of progress.

And there is pleasure in that.

This is what interests me: perhaps we sometimes defend a position not only because we believe it to be true, but because we like the person we are when we occupy it.

Psychology already describes much of the machinery behind this. Self-signaling concerns what our choices tell us about ourselves; motivated reasoning describes the way our motivations affect how we process arguments; identity-protective cognition helps explain why information becomes harder to accept when it threatens an identity we value. The older philosophical intuition is similar. La Rochefoucauld suspected our virtues of containing a considerable amount of amour-propre. Pascal was fascinated by our need to preserve a tolerable image of ourselves. Nietzsche repeatedly asked what psychological needs might hide behind proclaimed moral principles.

This does not mean that every conviction is secretly selfish. It means that a conviction can acquire a second value. Alongside “I believe this because I think it is true” appears another consideration: “I like being the person who believes this.” The compassionate one. The courageous one. The person who stands with the oppressed.

Once this happens, changing one's mind costs more than it did before.

If someone shows me that one of my positions is unjust, I should normally have discovered a reason to reconsider it. But if being just is part of my self-image, the objection now says something else as well: perhaps I am not quite the person I believe myself to be.

The argument has reached the self.

This may explain why apparently simple contradictions can become so difficult to acknowledge. We introduce another distinction, search for context, reinterpret evidence or change the argument. Not necessarily because we are consciously dishonest. The position may simply be carrying something that we do not want to lose.

Debate makes the mechanism visible

The same mechanism appears in disagreement. Someone may leave a discussion less certain than when he entered it while still refusing to concede anything publicly. Understanding a contradiction, privately revising one's position and saying “you were right” are three different things.

Pride can prevent the last step. But pride can also appear on the other side. If I continue arguing after the contradiction has been understood because I need the other person to acknowledge my victory, I may no longer be defending reason. I may be defending my image of myself as the rational one who won.

Sometimes the useful part of a debate is therefore over before anybody admits defeat. The contradiction has been made clear. The doubt has entered. The capitulation is something else.

Values should remain capable of judging us.

This suggests a different way of relating to values. It is more demanding to say “justice is something by which my actions should be judged” than “I am just.” Likewise, “human dignity is a principle against which I want my positions tested” says something different from “I am a humanist.”

The first formulation leaves open an uncomfortable possibility: I may fail my own principle.

That is precisely what a value should be able to do. It should sometimes embarrass us, contradict us and force us to abandon a position we enjoyed holding. Otherwise it risks becoming not a standard above us, but a mirror in which we admire ourselves.


II. A case study: the French radical left

This mechanism is not inherently left-wing. The conservative can admire himself for being patriotic. The contrarian for being independent. The rationalist for being lucid. The revolutionary for being courageous.

But these identities do not all carry the same moral prestige in contemporary Western public life. Calling oneself a humanist, feminist, anti-racist or defender of human rights contains an almost immediate moral compliment. Patriotism can also be a source of pride, but it is more politically contestable: depending on the context, it may raise questions about nationalism, immigration or exclusion. To call oneself a humanist usually requires much less explanation.

This makes parts of the contemporary Western left particularly interesting for this question. Its political identity is often expressed through values that are already morally affirmative.

La France insoumise makes this explicit in its own principles: “La France insoumise est un mouvement humaniste.” It associates that identity with human emancipation, popular sovereignty and social justice. Same thing for DeVillepin's 'La France Humaniste" for his presidential campaign.

The point is not that these values are insincere. The more interesting possibility is precisely that they may be sincere while also becoming part of the image people have of themselves. That is when contradictions become revealing.

Feminism, until the wrong women appear

The first example is broader than LFI itself and concerns part of the French activist left.

On 8 March 2024, several hundred members of the Jewish collective Nous Vivrons participated in the Paris march for International Women's Day. They came in particular to draw attention to Israeli women subjected to sexual violence during the 7 October attacks and to women still being held hostage. Their group had an official place in the procession. During the march they were insulted and targeted with projectiles; police eventually exfiltrated members of the collective. Paris police prefect Laurent Nuñez subsequently referred the incidents to prosecutors.

The scene is difficult to make more symbolic. A demonstration devoted to women's rights includes women trying to speak about rape and sexual violence committed against women, yet their presence becomes unacceptable to part of the same crowd because the Israeli-Palestinian conflict places them on the wrong side of another political division.

It raises a simple question: what comes first when two commitments conflict — the principle or the ideology?

That is the danger of moral self-contemplation: the principle can become less universal without the person ever ceasing to admire herself for holding it.

Humanism and “our heroes”

Jean-Luc Mélenchon's reaction to the death of Fidel Castro provides a different example.

In 2016, Mélenchon participated in a tribute to Castro in Paris. He spoke of the “example of our heroes” and, while acknowledging Castro's record, reduced the criticism to a striking formulation: “Fidel a fait des erreurs. Oui, mais tout le monde n'est pas Fidel.”

The word errors is worth noticing. Human Rights Watch describes Castro's nearly five decades of rule as a system that punished virtually all political dissent, imprisoned thousands, intimidated many more and denied generations of Cubans basic political freedoms. The same assessment also recognizes significant achievements in health and education.

The question is why repression becomes so easily surrounded with context when the repressive leader belongs to an admired political story.

Castro belongs to a narrative of revolution, resistance, anti-imperialism and emancipation. Once he occupies that place, the moral vocabulary changes. Acts that would produce immediate condemnation in an ideological opponent are historicized, contextualized or described as errors.

The facts have not disappeared. Their moral weight has changed.


When ideology comes before the principle

This mechanism can go further: ideology can come first, and the principle can be recruited afterward to justify it. International law is a particularly revealing example because its entire purpose is to constrain political preference. Mary Robinson, former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, regularly presents the rule of law as precisely such a constraint. Yet when she describes contested military actions as simply “illegal,” the legal argument on the other side cannot simply be skipped. If a state invokes Article 51 of the UN Charter and claims self-defence, that claim may ultimately be wrong, but anyone speaking in the name of international law has to confront it and explain why it fails. Otherwise the conclusion is political first and legal second.
At that point the direction has reversed: the law is no longer being used to test the ideology; the ideology has reached its conclusion and recruits the authority of law to certify it.

And that brings us back to the original problem.

Once humanist, feminist, anti-racist or defender of the rule of law becomes part of who I am, I acquire a psychological shortcut. I no longer need to ask with the same severity whether every position I hold actually satisfies those principles. I already know that I am the sort of person who represents them.

The uncomfortable women can be politically disqualified. The authoritarian hero can be historicized. My interpretation of the law can begin to sound like the law itself.

The value survives. More importantly, my image of myself as its bearer survives.

Perhaps the strongest test of a political value is therefore the moment at which it turns against one's own camp. Can my feminism defend women whose politics I despise? Can my humanism condemn a revolutionary leader I admire? Can I allow international law to contradict the political conclusion I wanted it to confirm? 

If not, perhaps I do not merely hold the value.

Perhaps I have made it part of the person I enjoy being.

And once that happens, protecting the value and protecting myself can become almost impossible to distinguish.
